title: Triangulation
description: Involving a third party—person, group, or institution—to create rivalry, jealousy, insecurity, or division, strengthening the manipulator’s control over both.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: Involving a third party—person, group, or institution—to create rivalry, jealousy, insecurity, or division, strengthening the manipulator’s control over both.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A partner constantly mentions an ex or a “close friend” of the opposite sex to make you feel competitive and insecure.
A parent tells one child “Your brother would never do this,” pitting siblings against each other for approval.
A boss plays two team members off each other, giving them conflicting information, so they fight while the boss remains the final arbiter.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Sharing private information between two parties to shape their views of each other.
Creating a “favorite” and a “scapegoat,” then rotating roles.
Dropping hints of outside admiration: “So-and-so thinks I’m amazing.”
The manipulator remains the center through whom all communication must flow.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “You’re lucky I chose you over him/her.”
“I told them what you said, and they agreed with me.”
“You should see how much she wants my attention.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You feel constantly compared to an invisible third party.
You’re competing for the attention or approval of one person.
You receive information about others only through the manipulator, never directly.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: It creates scarcity (their approval is a limited resource) and distracts from the manipulator’s own flaws. It isolates potential alliances between the two targets. It gives the triangulator a sense of power as the pivot point.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: If you’re being compared to someone else, refuse to engage: “I’m not in competition with anyone. Let’s talk about us.”
Verify information directly with the third party; do not accept hearsay.
In a work context, document and communicate openly with all parties to break the information monopoly.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Competing for the manipulator’s approval, which deepens the trap.
Confronting the third party based solely on the manipulator’s reports, which plays into their hands.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A boyfriend frequently mentions his female “best friend” who is supposedly funnier, more adventurous, and constantly texting him. His girlfriend feels inadequate and constantly seeks his reassurance. The “best friend” turns out to be a casual acquaintance he barely speaks to; he was inflating the connection to make his girlfriend feel insecure and easier to control.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Triangulation is a shadow play. The third party is often a prop, not a player. Don’t compete for a role in a script you didn’t write.
